beats.text: One point one five trillion dollars.
That's what OpenAI has reportedly promised to spend on computing power over the next decade.
Its revenue? About forty billion a year.
So who's paying for all of this?
Here's the strange part. The answer is a circle.
The companies building the AI boom are paying each other. Over and over.
In the next seven minutes, I'll show you every arrow in that circle.
Why some of the smartest investors alive are betting against it.
And why the people inside it say you're missing the point.
First, the scale. It's hard to overstate.
Last year, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent four hundred and ten billion dollars on AI infrastructure.
This year? Seven hundred and twenty five billion. Up seventy seven percent.
That's bigger than the entire economy of most countries.
Amazon alone is guiding to about two hundred and twenty billion. Alphabet, around two hundred. Microsoft, north of one seventy five. Meta, up to one forty five.
The big three clouds will spend about a hundred and two percent of their cloud revenue on capex.
Every dollar they earn goes straight back into concrete, chips, and power.
These aren't server rooms anymore. They're gigawatt campuses.
And UBS expects it to continue. Four point one trillion dollars of AI infrastructure through twenty twenty eight.
Where does that kind of money come from? Follow the arrows.
You only need seven names.
OpenAI buys the computing power. Nvidia sells the chips.
Oracle and CoreWeave build and rent the data centers.
AMD and Broadcom want a slice. Microsoft backs it all.
Now watch the arrows.
September twenty twenty five. Nvidia announces it intends to invest up to a hundred billion dollars in OpenAI.
So that OpenAI can buy Nvidia chips.
Imagine a car dealer lending you the money to buy his own cars.
Then OpenAI signs a three hundred billion dollar, five year deal with Oracle.
To deliver it, Oracle has to buy about forty billion dollars of Nvidia chips.
OpenAI gives AMD an order for six gigawatts of chips. AMD gives OpenAI the right to buy about ten percent of AMD.
And CoreWeave? Nvidia is its investor, its supplier, and its customer.
Same logos. Every arrow.
Why does that matter?
Because one dollar can be counted three times.
Investment on one balance sheet. Revenue on another. Growth on a third.
It's not necessarily fraud. But it's the exact pattern that haunted the telecom boom.
And here's the twist.
That hundred billion from Nvidia? Jensen Huang later said it was never a binding commitment.
By March, he said it was probably not in the cards.
So that loop loosened. The others didn't.
So who's actually paying? Increasingly, lenders.
Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle issued a hundred and ninety four billion dollars in bonds by late July.
That's already more than the hundred and eight billion they issued in all of last year.
Goldman Sachs expects around two hundred and fifty billion this year, and four hundred billion next year.
Spreads on long hyperscaler bonds have widened to about a hundred and eighteen basis points.
The bond market is getting tired.
Meta moved thirty billion dollars of data center financing into a joint venture, off its own balance sheet.
Oracle's free cash flow last fiscal year? Negative twenty three point seven billion dollars.
And banks reportedly struggled to sell thirty eight billion dollars of debt for one Oracle campus.
Then there's CoreWeave.
In February, a lender looked at a CoreWeave data center and said: we saw it. We passed.
CoreWeave's credit rating? B plus. Junk.
Every lender asks one question. Where does the money come from?
OpenAI lost over twenty one billion dollars last quarter. Though about twelve billion of that was non-cash.
It doesn't expect to be cash flow positive until twenty thirty.
Its commitments are roughly twenty times its annual spending.
And a twenty twenty five MIT report found that ninety five percent of corporate AI pilots showed no measurable profit impact.
Critics say that headline is misread. But the point stands. Adoption is lagging the buildout.
Michael Burry, the man who shorted the housing market, is betting against Nvidia.
His argument isn't demand. It's accounting.
Cloud giants say an AI chip lasts five to six years. Burry says two to three.
If he's right, profits are overstated by about a hundred and seventy six billion dollars through twenty twenty eight.
Nvidia's CEO disagrees. And six year old A one hundred chips still resell for around five thousand dollars.
But here's why the optimists aren't scared.
Anthropic's run rate hit sixty five billion dollars in July. Seven times last year.
Add OpenAI's forty billion. That's about a hundred billion a year. From almost nothing three years ago.
And unlike the dot-com bubble, these chips aren't sitting idle.
Cloud executives keep saying they can't build fast enough.
Even if one tenant fails, land, power, and buildings don't vanish. Someone else moves in.
Still, we've seen this movie.
Nineteen ninety nine. Up to two trillion dollars poured into fiber optic cable.
By two thousand two, only two point seven percent of it was lit.
Bandwidth prices collapsed. Global Crossing and WorldCom went bankrupt.
But that dark fiber later carried Netflix, the cloud, and the modern internet.
The infrastructure won. The investors who built it mostly didn't.
So what if one link snaps?
CoreWeave can't refinance. Its lenders take losses. Nvidia, as supplier and shareholder, takes a hit.
OpenAI's growth slows. Oracle is stuck with capacity built for one customer.
The shockwave runs backward along every arrow.
Lenders, suppliers and shareholders get hit first. Not the person using the chatbot.
So watch three things.
Nvidia's earnings, for any crack in chip demand.
The ratio of OpenAI and Anthropic revenue to their compute commitments.
And the credit ratings of the data center borrowers. Starting with CoreWeave and Oracle.
Nobody knows yet if this is nineteen ninety six or nineteen ninety nine.
Whichever way it breaks, you've now seen the wiring.
Subscribe, and tell me what to break down next. The custom chip war, or the data center power crisis.
